seo.title: Karmic tail 3 10 16 compatibility: a garden, a wheel and lightning
seo.description: Karmic tail 3 10 16 compatibility: The Empress, the Wheel of Fortune and The Tower. Why a turning wheel stands where the Sun should be, and how to work it out.

title: The couple's tail 3-10-16: The Empress, the Wheel of Fortune and The Tower in compatibility
short: The karmic tail 3-10-16 in compatibility begins with a garden and ends with lightning. Between them the arithmetic of the matrix leaves room for only two cards, The Sun or the Wheel of Fortune, and in almost three couples out of four with these two ends it is the Wheel. This is the tail of a couple who want to grow abundance together, live that wish through turns in which one rises while the other sinks, and learn the main thing: how to survive the collapse of what they invented — the image of the partner and of their shared future — and remain one tree.

sections.h2: The chestnut by its old roots: the novel where tail 3-10-16 lives
paragraphs: Many readers know the story. Jane, an orphan, works as a governess at Thornfield Hall. Its master, Mr Rochester, is twenty years older and stands so high on the English ladder of rank that between them, in Jane's words, lies "the wider ocean—wealth, caste, custom".

Chapter 23. Midsummer Eve, sunset. Jane goes out into the orchard: "No nook in the grounds more sheltered and more Eden-like." She sees "trees laden with ripening fruit"; Rochester takes "a ripe cherry from the wall". Down the laurel walk he leads her to a giant horse-chestnut: "here is the chestnut tree: here is the bench at its old roots." On that bench he proposes, and Jane feels herself "called to the paradise of union".

Then the chestnut "writhed and groaned", wind roars down the walk, a spark leaps out of a cloud — "a crack, a crash, and a close rattling peal". In the morning little Adèle runs in with the news: "the great horse-chestnut at the bottom of the orchard had been struck by lightning in the night, and half of it split away."

One night holds the whole tail in miniature. The garden where two people agree on their future is The Empress. Weather that overturns within the hour is the Wheel. Lightning in the very tree at whose roots the "yes" was spoken is The Tower. The novel then unfolds the same three acts over a year: the wedding will be stopped at the altar, Jane will leave with nothing, fortune will raise her and bring him down, Thornfield will burn. And Brontë does not forget the tree until her last chapters.

On the eve of the wedding Jane goes back to it: "The cloven halves were not broken from each other, for the firm base and strong roots kept them unsundered below; though community of vitality was destroyed… as yet, however, they might be said to form one tree—a ruin, but an entire ruin." And she speaks to the wreckage as if it were alive: "You did right to hold fast to each other."

A year later the blinded Rochester will say of himself: "I am no better than the old lightning-struck chestnut-tree in Thornfield orchard." Jane will answer with the sentence that closes the tail: "You are no ruin, sir—no lightning-struck tree… Plants will grow about your roots." A garden at the entry, lightning in the main task — and a garden again, this time around a split trunk. The cards show how a couple gets there.

sections.h2: Entry to the task: The Empress and two dialects of one garden
paragraphs: M is the Entry to the task. For Lisovskaya it holds the couple's shared wishes and agreements, their "common language"; in the reading the same point also appears in the sphere Relationship and common language. The point lies on the line of tasks, so the wish with which a couple enters the task easily becomes resistance.

Here the wish is The Empress: to grow. A home, a family, a shared venture, a move closer to the land, an "our" budget, the feeling of a full cup. Jane and Rochester share the wish but speak it in different dialects.

Jane's dialect is home as a person. Coming back to Thornfield, she blurts out: "wherever you are is my home—my only home." Rochester's dialect is home as a gift. The morning after the proposal he has already written to his banker for the family jewels and hopes "to pour them into your lap": "the diamond chain round your neck, and the circlet on your forehead", bracelets, rings, satin and lace. Jane replies: "And then you won't know me, sir… an ape in a harlequin's jacket." At the silk warehouse he picks an amethyst silk and a pink satin; she fights him down to black satin and pearl-grey silk, and Rochester vows "he would yet see me glittering like a parterre".

Jane states her terms in words that could hang over any joint budget: "I will not be your English Céline Varens." Céline was Rochester's former mistress, a French opera-dancer he had showered with diamonds. "I shall continue to act as Adèle's governess; by that I shall earn my board and lodging, and thirty pounds a year besides… and you shall give me nothing but— … Your regard; and if I give you mine in return, that debt will be quit."

Beneath The Empress hides a second role. Rochester asks Jane for more than her hand. Three chapters before the proposal he asks her, as if about some abstract man, whether "the wandering and sinful, but now rest-seeking and repentant, man" may bind a gentle stranger to himself for ever, "thereby securing his own peace of mind and regeneration of life". On the night of the proposal he repeats: "It will atone—it will atone." Waite calls The Empress "not Regina coeli, but she is still refugium peccatorum" — the refuge of sinners. That is exactly the post Rochester offers Jane. She declines it in advance: **"a wanderer's repose or a sinner's reformation should never depend on a fellow-creature."**

Among the reasons The Empress brings a couple together Lisovskaya lists this one too: to thaw after past unhappy relationships. On the bright side the union really does warm. On the dark side one partner enters it as a shelter, and the other is handed the duty of being the garden where the first will be saved. In daily life it looks ordinary: "after everything I've been through, you're all I live for", "why work, I'll give you everything", gifts that leave the other feeling in debt, and a quiet separate account the other opens so as not to be kept.

Jane opens exactly such an account. Driving home from the shops, she remembers her uncle in Madeira, who once meant to make her his heir: "if I had ever so small an independency; I never can bear being dressed like a doll by Mr. Rochester, or sitting like a second Danae with the golden shower falling daily round me." That same day she writes to tell her uncle about the marriage. The letter reaches him while Mason is staying with him — the brother of Rochester's first wife, of whom Jane knows nothing. A few weeks later Mason and a solicitor stop the wedding. **The Empress's wish not to enter the union empty-handed is what sets the Wheel turning, and the Wheel brings the lightning.** Wen pins the same shadow to The Empress: her fruition "might also be a foreshadowing of unintended or unanticipated consequences".

Even Danaë is the right choice. Horace's ode (III.16) opens with "Inclusam Danaen turris aenea" — "Danaë, shut in a tower of bronze" (our translation, as with the Latin below). Horace goes on to say that gold loves to pass through guards and to break through rock "more powerfully than the lightning's stroke", that a seer's house fell "for gain", and he sums up: "Multa petentibus desunt multa" — those who seek much lack much. One ode holds gold, a tower and lightning. At the entry to the task Jane fears that the garden she is being given will turn out to be a bronze tower with a golden shower inside.

sections.h2: Why the Sun is not between the garden and the lightning
paragraphs: In a personal matrix the middle of the tail is the sum of the entry and the main task. By that formula The Sun would stand between The Empress and The Tower: 3 + 16 = 19. In a couple the middle is not derived from the two ends; it is added up from the personal middles of two people. But addition has a memory. Reducing a number does not change its remainder after division by nine, so by that remainder the couple's middle always matches the sum of entry and task. With an entry of 3 and a task of 16, only two cards are allowed in the middle: 19 or 10 (28 reduces to 10).

So couples with The Empress at the entry and The Tower as the task have only this choice: The Sun or the Wheel. Tail 3-19-16 occurs in 1.26% of couples, 3-10-16 in 3.35%. **In almost three cases out of four what stands between the garden and the lightning is not steady light but a turn.**

The Sun does not vanish from the people themselves. In half of the couples with this tail (49%) one partner carries it in the middle of their own tail: their personal tail is 12-19-7. In the couple this Sun is added to the other partner's nine, The Hermit, and becomes the Wheel: 19 + 9 = 28 → 10. The light of one does not shine evenly on both — it starts to rotate. This is our reading; the arithmetic is checked by going through all birth dates.

Brontë got there first here too. Rochester, speaking of himself as if of a stranger, says: "your sun at noon darkens in an eclipse, which you feel will not leave it till the time of setting." A month before the wedding Jane writes of Rochester: "He stood between me and every thought of religion, as an eclipse intervenes between man and the broad sun… of whom I had made an idol." Each of the two has an eclipse. And on the evening before the wedding Jane catches herself thinking that "my fortune had passed its meridian, and must now decline". The meridian is the highest point, where the sun stands at noon. The Sun reaches its height, and then the wheel begins.

sections.h2: Middle of the task: the Wheel on which two change places
paragraphs: N is the Middle of the task. Lisovskaya gives this point no meaning of its own: it adds to the main task. In our reading the middle shows how a couple lives the road from the wish to the task. In 3-10-16 that road is the Wheel: highs and lows take turns, and what matters most in this energy, for Lisovskaya, is to accept the change itself rather than fight it.

Above all, the Wheel does one thing to this couple: it makes the two change places. At Thornfield Rochester is the master. He has the estate, the money and the right to decide where the governess goes: on the night of the proposal he first tells her she will have to go to Ireland. Jane, as he puts it himself, is in a "responsible and dependent position". A year later it is all reversed. Jane has inherited a fortune, and when Rochester asks who will look after her now, she answers: **"I am independent, sir, as well as rich: I am my own mistress."** Rochester is blind, his left arm maimed; he lives in a house buried in a wood and calls himself "a blind lameter".

Brontë even names the turn with a card word. Hearing about the twenty thousand pounds, Jane thinks: "Here was a new card turned up! It is a fine thing, reader, to be lifted in a moment from indigence to wealth." Indigence is a word from Waite's list for The Tower, while "abundance" is on his list for the reversed Wheel. The Wheel in the middle of the tail carries the couple from The Tower's word to The Empress's and back.

And at once it is clear which dialect of the garden Jane speaks now. She finds cousins: "This was wealth indeed!—wealth to the heart!… not like the ponderous gift of gold." She divides the inheritance four ways: "Twenty thousand pounds shared equally would be five thousand each, justice—enough and to spare."

The Wheel has a dark side as well, and in the novel Rochester plays it out. He turns the wheel himself to test feelings. He lets a rumour spread that "my fortune was not a third of what was supposed" and watches the society beauty everyone took for his bride grow cold. Disguised as a gypsy fortune-teller, he tells Jane her fortune and probes whether she is waiting for him: "Chance has meted you a measure of happiness… It depends on yourself to stretch out your hand, and take it up." Among the Wheel's tasks Lisovskaya lists leaving manipulation and grudges behind, no longer blaming fate and each other, accepting the partner with their flaws, looking for solutions instead of complaints. A test by turning the wheel is the same attempt to steer the wheel instead of living on it.

In the life of a 3-10-16 couple the turns look ordinary. One loses a job while the other is promoted the same year. The one who always carried the load suddenly needs support. A good year gives way to a hard one, quiet to a quarrel, and the argument is no longer about the matter but about places: "you've changed", "you used to be stronger", "now you're keeping me". The test of the middle is not to fix each other in the roles of the first act: master and governess, provider and the one provided for. A place on the wheel is a place, not a character. Rochester knows it from experience: "Fortune has knocked me about since: she has even kneaded me with her knuckles, and now I flatter myself I am hard and tough as an India-rubber ball."

One more detail from the numbers. In a quarter of couples with this tail the partners' personal tails are identical: both have 15-5-8. Their Wheel is made of two identical Hierophants (5 + 5 = 10). The turn is not born from the two being different — the union itself creates it.

sections.h2: Main task: The Tower strikes what was invented
paragraphs: D is the Main task. It is read mostly through its shadow side: what the couple cannot manage and what it has to learn. In Lisovskaya's card for The Tower the first of the couple's tasks is **the collapse of an invented image of the partner**, and her key to the energy is that trials lived through together make the union stronger.

In Jane Eyre both of them are invented. Rochester invents Jane: he calls her a fairy, an elf, "you almost unearthly thing", wants to dress her in satin and "make the world acknowledge you a beauty". Jane invents Rochester, and calls it an idol herself. On the eve of the wedding she shuts the wardrobe on her wedding dress with "I will leave you by yourself, white dream", and cannot bring herself to fix the address cards marked "Mrs. Rochester" to her trunks: "Mrs. Rochester! She did not exist: she would not be born till to-morrow." In the morning it turns out that a Mrs Rochester has existed for years. Rochester is married; his mad wife Bertha is kept locked up on the third storey of Thornfield. The lightning struck the image of the future wife — literally.

What Jane writes after the wedding that never happened is an exact formula for The Tower in a couple: **"Mr. Rochester was not to me what he had been; for he was not what I had thought him."** Right after it comes The Empress's whole garden, turned over by the Wheel in a single night: "A Christmas frost had come at midsummer; a white December storm had whirled over June; ice glazed the ripe apples, drifts crushed the blowing roses; on hayfield and cornfield lay a frozen shroud."

Later the tower falls in the literal sense too. Bertha sets the house on fire and throws herself from the battlements. Rochester will not leave until everyone else is out, and on the staircase the house comes down on him. When Jane returns, she sees what she once saw in a dream: of the front only a tall, fragile wall is left, "no roof, no battlements, no chimneys—all had crashed in".

In real life this Tower does not have to be a catastrophe. More often the blow lands on the picture. A partner does something "not like them". An old secret or a debt comes out. The plan for a house, a move, a shared venture — the plan around which "we" was built — collapses. The Tower's shadow side for Lisovskaya is that at such moments the two look in different directions: one rescues the plan, the other rescues themselves. They lose their temper, throw out words in shock that are hard to take back, threaten to leave in order to hold on. The task is not to keep the lightning from striking. The task is to tell the person apart from the picture each has painted of them, and to let the picture fall rather than the person.

sections.h2: What Waite drew: a field, a wheel's rim and a sun on the forehead
paragraphs: The cards on this site have their own artwork. But the Waite–Smith deck, and Wen's commentary on it, hold four details that read as clues to this tail.
**The Empress.** In front of her, Waite writes, "a field of corn is ripening". In Brontë, after the wedding that never happened, a frozen shroud lies on the cornfield.

**The Wheel.** Waite drew the card after Lévi's reconstruction, with "a Hermanubis rising with the wheel" and "a Typhon on the descending side"; Waite "presented Typhon in his serpent form". Two figures on one rim, and one goes up exactly when the other goes down. That is Jane and Rochester in the second year of their story.

**The Tower.** Waite argues against reading the card as the chastisement of pride: such readings, he says, do not "account for the two persons who are the living sufferers". Two people fall. And Wen, describing the card, writes: "Yellowing leaves from the Tree of Life float down from the heavens." The Tower has a tree as well.

**Temperance, the centre of these couples.** Waite's angel has "the sign of the sun upon his forehead". Waite adds that it is "untrue to say that the figure symbolizes the genius of the sun, though it is the analogy of solar light". The Sun that is missing from the middle of the tail is painted on the forehead of the couple's centre.

sections.h2: An entire ruin: what holds the two halves
paragraphs: The main secret of this tail is written in its numbers. The centre of the matrix in 3-10-16 couples is Temperance, 14, practically always: The Hierophant stands in the centre for four couples in ten thousand. And 16 + 14 = 30, which reduces to 3. **The main task added to the couple's atmosphere gives exactly the entry.** In a personal matrix every tail is built this way: the entry equals the main task plus the centre. A 3-10-16 couple obeys the same rule. Lightning plus what the two patiently blend between them gives back the garden.

For Lisovskaya the couple's centre is their shared atmosphere, what happens between two people when nobody is watching. Wen writes of Temperance as forces that "restore what was lost, cool what was too hot, heat up what was too cold". Lisovskaya's shadow side of this centre is just as precise: one always gives way, and the other never even thinks of it. Temperance breaks when only one of them is doing the blending.

Brontë shows it in a small thing. Walking away from the split chestnut, Jane gathers up "the apples with which the grass round the tree roots was thickly strewn" and divides "the ripe from the unripe". The garden goes on at the roots of the struck tree. The last word on Waite's list for The Tower is "ruin", and that is exactly what Brontë calls the chestnut: a ruin, but an entire one.

At the end of the novel a gesture from the beginning comes back. Their first meeting is a fall: on an icy road, "Man and horse were down". Rochester has sprained his ankle and says: "necessity compels me to make you useful." He "laid a heavy hand on my shoulder, and leaning on me with some stress, limped to his horse". In the wood at Ferndean, blind now, he "stretched his hand out to be led", and Jane lets it pass round her shoulder: "I served both for his prop and guide." The first fall and the last support are one movement, only now it is not made out of necessity.

Jane's answer about the chestnut, in full: "You are no ruin, sir—no lightning-struck tree: you are green and vigorous. Plants will grow about your roots, whether you ask them or not, because they take delight in your bountiful shadow; and as they grow they will lean towards you, and wind round you, because your strength offers them so safe a prop." And the sum of ten years of marriage: "To be together is for us to be at once as free as in solitude, as gay as in company. We talk, I believe, all day long: to talk to each other is but a more animated and an audible thinking." The common language with which the couple entered the task has become the air they breathe. "Perfect concord", Jane writes, and that is a word for Temperance.

In the penultimate chapter Rochester thanks God that, "in the midst of judgment, he has remembered mercy". Wen's description of the reversed Tower has a similar line: "There will be mercy and some will be saved."

sections.h2: The couple's values: The Lovers or The Devil
paragraphs: The Couple's values sphere is the spiritual purpose, what the union exists for. In couples with tail 3-10-16 it holds The Lovers (69.5%) or The Devil (30.5%). Matching them with the novel is our reading.

On the night of the proposal Jane breaks out of Rochester's arms: "I am no bird; and no net ensnares me; I am a free human being with an independent will." Rochester replies: "And your will shall decide your destiny." Will and destiny — The Lovers and the Wheel in one line. For such a couple the value of The Lovers is a choice made again after every turn, not once under the chestnut. The last chapter opens with "Reader, I married him", and the subject of that sentence is she.

The Devil is a chain. In the same weeks Rochester jokes that once he has her, he will "—figuratively speaking—attach you to a chain like this", touching his watch-guard. Jane refuses two chains: life with Rochester without marriage after the broken wedding, and marriage without love to St John Rivers ("I scorn your idea of love"). Lisovskaya's closing thought on The Devil is that no one belongs to anyone. Brontë says the same from inside a marriage: "I am my husband's life as fully as he is mine." When both belong to each other, it is no longer a chain.

sections.h2: How tail 3-10-16 is worked out: 05.07.1975 and 14.09.1975
paragraphs: Each point of the couple's matrix is the sum of the same points in the two personal matrices, reduced to 22. The couple's tail is assembled from two personal tails: entry with entry, middle with middle, task with task. A person born on 05.07.1975 has the personal tail 12-19-7; a person born on 14.09.1975 has 18-9-9.

By the personal formula, this couple's entry plus task would give 3 + 16 = 19, The Sun. But the couple's middle is 19 + 9, the middles of two people, and the first partner's Sun literally becomes the Wheel here. Elsewhere in this couple's matrix the centre is 5 + 9 = 14, Temperance; The Devil stands in Values; The Sun (19) stands on Image of the couple, which is how others see them, and that happens in 4.3% of couples with this tail. What to create together holds The Tower again (16), as in 6.8% of such couples: a couple whose main task is The Tower is also called to build together.
What a run through every birth date since 1900 showed:

ul: **Frequency.** Tail 3-10-16 occurs in one couple in 30 (3.353%), sixth place among the 97 couple tails.

**Where the cards come from.** Four combinations of personal tails: 12-19-7 + 18-9-9 (49% of such couples), 15-5-8 + 15-5-8 (25%), 15-20-5 + 15-8-11 (25%) and the vanishingly rare 21-10-7 + 9-18-9 (0.04%).

**No one's and shared.** In 99.96% of such couples none of the three tail cards appears in either partner's personal tail. The Empress at the entry always comes from 30 (12 + 18, 15 + 15 or 21 + 9): no one brings an Empress of their own to the entry. The Tower is always an exact sum with no reduction: 7 + 9, 8 + 8 or 5 + 11. The whole tail is born between two people.
**Centre.** Temperance in 99.96% of couples; The Hierophant only in the rarest, fourth combination.
**Values.** The Lovers in 69.5%, The Devil in 30.5%.

paragraphs: In couples with two identical 15-5-8 tails each card of the couple is a doubled card of each partner: two Devils make The Empress (15 + 15 = 30 → 3), two Hierophants make the Wheel, two Justices make The Tower (8 + 8 = 16). If two people are equally sure they know what is fair, together they risk building the very tower that will be struck. This is our reading.

sections.h2: What helps a couple with tail 3-10-16

ul: **Divide the garden into two plots.** Each has their own work, their own income, their own "thirty pounds a year". Abundance that one gives and the other only receives turns, at this entry, into a golden shower inside a bronze tower.

**Do not appoint the partner as a refuge.** One person's peace should not depend wholly on the other. Friends, one's own work, support outside the couple; with the Wheel, Lisovskaya advises not to close in on each other.
**Call a place on the wheel a place.** "Things are hard for you right now" instead of "you've become weak". The roles of the early years — who earns, who decides, who takes care — are not for life.
**Do not test by turning the wheel.** A rumour of ruin, a question like "if I lost everything, would you stay?" — that is an attempt to spin the wheel by hand. An answer comes, and trust shrinks.
**When the blow comes, look in one direction first.** The first hours are not for verdicts or decisions. First "what has happened to us", then, if it is still needed, "whose fault was it".
**Tell the person apart from the picture.** Ask what in the ruins was one's own invention. Jane's line "he was not what I had thought him" is the start of the work, not its end.
**Build from the root.** After the blow, list what is still alive: conversations, shared jokes, the habit of leaning on the other's shoulder. The new garden grows from there.

paragraphs: If the blow is threats, violence, or fear for oneself or for the children, it is not "The Tower's lesson". That calls for help: a local emergency number or a crisis line.

ul: **3 · The Empress — entry to the task.** The couple's common language is the language of growth: a home, a family, a shared venture, plenty. The couple enters the task with this wish, and the same wish turns into resistance when one wants to give the other a garden and the other wants to grow one of their own.

**10 · The Wheel of Fortune — middle of the task.** The path does not run in even sunlight but in turns: whoever was on top ends up below, and the other way round. The test of the middle is not to mistake a place on the wheel for a character.
**16 · The Tower — main task.** The lightning does not strike the couple; it strikes what each of them invented. The task is to let the picture fall and keep the root.

intro: This tail has a novel in which all three cards stand in a single scene. In Charlotte Brontë's Jane Eyre (1847) the proposal is made in a garden, on a bench by the old roots of a chestnut tree, and that night lightning strikes the chestnut.

faq.q: What does the program 3-10-16 mean in the destiny matrix?
faq.a: In the destiny matrix a program is a stable combination of three arcana; Lisovskaya also calls the tail of a couple's matrix a karmic program. The numbers 3-10-16 are a couple's tail. The entry to the task is The Empress: a shared wish to grow a home, a venture, plenty. The middle is the Wheel of Fortune: a road through turns in which the partners change places. The main task is The Tower: the collapse of the invented image of the partner and of the shared future, and the ability to stay together after it.

Both have the same ends, The Empress and The Tower, but a different middle, and with these ends the middle can only be The Sun or the Wheel. In 3-19-16 the road runs through The Sun, steady growth in the light; that tail occurs in 1.26% of couples. In 3-10-16 the road runs through a turn in which one rises and the other sinks; it occurs in 3.35% of couples, almost three times as often.

faq.q: Can tail 3-10-16 appear in a personal matrix?
faq.a: No. In a personal matrix the middle of the tail equals the sum of the entry and the task, so with 3 and 16 it would be 19. What is more, in a person's matrix The Tower as the main task appears only in the tail 21-10-16, where the Wheel also stands before it and The World stands at the entry. Tail 3-10-16 appears only when two matrices are added together.

faq.q: Is tail 3-10-16 a bad sign for a couple?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail does not predict events and passes no verdict on the union. It shows where the main test lies: wherever the two of them hold an invented image. Lisovskaya's key to The Tower in a couple is that trials lived through together make the union stronger. And in the numbers of this tail, The Tower together with the couple's atmosphere gives back The Empress.

report: In Charlotte Brontë's Jane Eyre the proposal is made in a garden, on a bench by the old roots of a giant chestnut. That same night lightning strikes the chestnut, and by morning half of it has split away. One night holds the whole of tail 3-10-16: the garden where two people agree on their future is The Empress; weather that overturns within the hour is the Wheel of Fortune; the blow to the very tree at whose roots the "yes" was spoken is The Tower. And Brontë gives her main answer a year later, when she comes back to the tree.

report.h3: A garden to be given, and a garden to be grown

report: The entry to the task is The Empress. It is the couple's common language, the wish to grow something together: a home, a family, a shared venture, a full cup. The two lovers share the wish but speak it in different dialects. For Jane home is a person: her home is wherever he is, and she has no other. For Rochester home is a gift. The morning after the proposal he sends for the family jewels and drags her to the silk warehouse. Jane sets terms that would suit any joint budget: "I shall continue to act as Adèle's governess; by that I shall earn my board and lodging, and thirty pounds a year besides."

Beneath The Empress hides a second role. Rochester looks to Jane for the "regeneration of life", and on the night of the proposal he repeats: "It will atone—it will atone." Waite calls The Empress refugium peccatorum, the refuge of sinners. Jane declines the post in advance: **"a wanderer's repose or a sinner's reformation should never depend on a fellow-creature."** On the dark side of this entry one partner comes into the union as into a shelter, and the other is obliged to be the garden where the first will be saved.

And the entry itself sets everything else in motion. So as not to sit "like a second Danae" under a golden shower, Jane writes to her uncle in Madeira: she wants to enter the marriage with something of her own. The letter reaches the brother of Rochester's first wife, of whom Jane knows nothing, and a few weeks later the wedding is stopped at the altar. **The Empress's wish is what sets the Wheel turning, and the Wheel brings the lightning.**

report.h3: Between the garden and the lightning: a wheel, not a sun

report: By the arithmetic of a single person, The Sun would stand between The Empress and The Tower — steady light. In the couple the Wheel stands there, and it makes the two change places. At Thornfield Rochester is the master, and Jane is in a "dependent position". A year later she inherits a fortune and says: "I am independent, sir, as well as rich: I am my own mistress." He has gone blind and calls himself "a blind lameter". Brontë even names the turn with a card word: "Here was a new card turned up!"

The sun in the novel is covered twice. Rochester speaks of a sun that "at noon darkens in an eclipse". Jane writes that he stood between her and God "as an eclipse intervenes between man and the broad sun", and that she had made an idol of him. On the eve of the wedding she feels that her fortune "had passed its meridian, and must now decline".

In everyday life such turns are ordinary. One loses a job, the other is promoted. The one who always carried the load suddenly needs support. The argument is no longer about the matter but about places: who has changed, who is keeping whom. The test of the middle is not to fix each other in the roles of the early years. A place on the wheel is a place, not a character. Rochester plays out the Wheel's dark side himself: he lets a rumour spread that his fortune is "not a third of what was supposed", to test someone's feelings. A test by turning the wheel is an attempt to spin the wheel by hand.

report.h3: The lightning strikes what was invented

report: The main task is The Tower, and it is read through its shadow side: the collapse of an invented image of the partner. Here both are invented. Rochester calls Jane a fairy and an elf and wants to dress her in satin. Jane has made herself an idol. On the eve of the wedding she cannot bring herself to fix the address cards for the new bride to her trunks: "Mrs. Rochester! She did not exist: she would not be born till to-morrow." In the morning it turns out that a Mrs Rochester has existed for years. After the wedding that never happened, Jane writes down the formula of this Tower: **"he was not what I had thought him."** And the whole garden freezes overnight: "A Christmas frost had come at midsummer… ice glazed the ripe apples."

In real life this Tower does not have to be a catastrophe. The blow lands on the picture: a partner does something "not like them", an old secret comes out, the plan around which "we" was built collapses. At such moments the two look in different directions and throw out words that are hard to take back. The task is to tell the person apart from the picture and to let the picture fall rather than the person.

report.h3: A ruin, but an entire one

report: On the eve of the wedding Jane walks up to the split chestnut. The cloven halves have not broken from each other: the firm base and strong roots hold them together below, and for now it is still one tree — **"a ruin, but an entire ruin"**. Jane tells the wreckage, as if it were alive, that the halves did right to hold fast to each other. Then she gathers up the apples strewn round the roots.

The numbers of the tail say the same. The centre of such couples holds Temperance, the shared atmosphere, what the two patiently blend between them. The Tower together with Temperance gives exactly The Empress: lightning plus that blending gives back the garden.

Their first meeting is a fall: Rochester and his horse go down on an icy road, and he gets back to the saddle leaning on Jane's shoulder. At the end, blind now, he stretches out his hand to be led, and Jane lets it pass round her shoulder: "I served both for his prop and guide." When he compares himself to the old chestnut, Jane answers that he is no ruin and that plants will grow about his roots. She sums up the marriage like this: "to talk to each other is but a more animated and an audible thinking." The common language with which the entry began has become the air the couple breathes.

What helps: each partner keeps their own work and their own income; the partner is not a refuge; a place on the wheel is called a place; in the first hours after a blow, no verdicts, and both look in one direction; rebuilding starts from what is still alive. If the blow is threats, violence or fear for oneself, it is not "The Tower's lesson": it calls for help, a local emergency number or a crisis line.
